title: Root Q3 Profit Hits $14.4M as Revenue Slips and Policies Grow
summary: Root reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $14.4 million against a $5.4 million loss a year earlier, with a gross combined ratio of 96.8%, while gross written premium fell 8% to $357.5 million as the insurer held back on direct auto growth.
description:
Root, Inc., the Ohio-based auto insurer that prices policies using driving data from a smartphone app, reported a profit for the third quarter of 2026. Net income was $14.4 million, or $0.86 a diluted share, against a net loss of $5.4 million, or $0.35 a share, a year earlier. At the same time, revenue slipped to $381.3 million from $387.8 million. This article walks through the numbers in the company's shareholder letter, which was filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and explains why a fall in premium can sit alongside a better profit. It is a summary of company-reported results and not investment advice.

The headline numbers

The shareholder letter reports gross written premium of $357.5 million for the quarter, down from $387.2 million a year earlier, a drop of about 8%. Gross premiums earned, which recognise premium as coverage is provided, were $356.0 million against $373.1 million, a fall of about 5%. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, was $33.5 million against $33.7 million. Direct contribution, another non-GAAP measure the company uses to gauge the profitability of its book before reinsurance and fixed costs, was $119.9 million against $127.4 million.

The improvement in earnings came from underwriting. The gross combined ratio, which adds claims and expenses as a share of premium, was 96.8% against 101.3% a year earlier. A combined ratio below 100% means the insurer made an underwriting profit before investment income. The net combined ratio, after reinsurance, was 97.2% against 102.1%. The gross loss ratio was 58.0% against 58.5%. The gross accident-period loss ratio, which counts claims from events in the quarter regardless of when they are reported, rose to 61.1% from 56.5%, a detail worth watching because it points to somewhat higher claims from the current period.

More policies, lower premium per policy

Policies in force rose to 484,037 from 466,320, an increase of about 4%. Premium per policy fell to $1,441 from $1,581. That combination explains the revenue picture: Root insured more vehicles but charged less on average. The letter says large carriers increased marketing and lowered average premiums, creating a competitive market. In that setting Root says it was disciplined about capital, and it "intentionally" traded off growth in its direct channel when expected returns fell below its threshold. Direct contribution fell, which is consistent with a smaller direct business at lower average prices.

Partnerships carry more of the growth

Root's strategy leans on embedded insurance, meaning policies sold at the point where a customer is already making another purchase. The letter says partnership new writings, including independent agents, grew 19% year over year, and that these channels were 52% of total new writings, up from 44%. It also says the company renewed and extended its commercial relationship with Carvana through August 2028, and that more than 250,000 Root policies were written through Carvana's integrated experience between September 2022 and August 2026.

A new pilot is the Hyundai Secure+ Powered by Root programme, launched in 14 Phoenix-area dealerships. According to the letter, eligible customers who finance or lease a new Hyundai through Hyundai Capital America receive six months of Root auto insurance at no cost. The letter does not say what the programme costs Root or what it expects it to add. The shareholder letter also lists Toyota, Experian and Jerry among its partners.

Footprint and technology

Root said it is active in 38 auto markets, covering about 82% of the US population. It added New Jersey in July 2026 and Wyoming in October 2026. On technology, chief executive Alex Timm said the company began deploying a new proprietary pricing model in the fourth quarter of 2026, which the company expects to deliver its largest improvement in predictive power to date. The letter also points to artificial intelligence for end-to-end automation and to connected-vehicle experiences. These are management statements of intent, and the results of the pricing model will show up only in later quarters.

Capital and buybacks

Cash and cash equivalents were $596.3 million at September 30, 2026, compared with $669.3 million at the end of 2025, and restricted cash was $75.3 million. Long-term debt was $197.5 million. Root repurchased $36.2 million of its shares during the quarter under a $75 million authorisation. The letter does not provide numeric guidance for 2026. Annualised return on equity was about 18%, according to the company.

How to read the quarter

Three points help put the numbers in context. First, the swing to a profit is real in the sense that the combined ratio crossed below 100%, but one quarter does not make a trend, and the accident-period loss ratio moved the other way. Second, shrinking premium is a choice as much as a result. Root's own statement says it gave up some direct growth. Whether that choice pays off depends on whether prices in the market stabilise. Third, the company's reliance on partners such as Carvana and Hyundai means its growth is tied to the health of those relationships, including the renewal through 2028 that the letter highlights.

What it means for drivers

Drivers who shop for auto insurance have seen a market in which several large carriers are spending heavily to attract customers. A smaller carrier choosing to hold back suggests that low prices carry a cost to insurers, which can show up later in rates, availability or underwriting rules. Policyholders can compare quotes and check how telematics or usage-based programmes use their data before they sign up.

What to watch next

Readers following the company should watch the next shareholder letter for whether policies in force keep rising while premium per policy stabilises, whether the accident-period loss ratio continues to climb, and how the Hyundai pilot and the new pricing model perform. Root publishes its filings on its investor relations site and on the SEC website. This article summarises public company statements and is not financial advice.

The gross combined ratio improved to 96.8% from 101.3%, and the net combined ratio to 97.2% from 102.1%, while the gross loss ratio was 58.0% against 58.5%.
Gross written premium fell 8% to $357.5 million and gross premiums earned fell 5% to $356.0 million, even though policies in force rose 4% to 484,037.

Its results show how a smaller carrier is trading premium growth for underwriting profit while larger competitors spend more on marketing and cut prices, which affects the choices drivers see.

title: Oscar Health Q3: $167M Profit and Third Raise to 2026 Outlook
summary: Oscar Health reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $167.3 million on revenue of $5.14 billion, with a medical loss ratio of 84.0%, and raised its full-year earnings from operations outlook to $850 million to $950 million, helped by a $250 million risk adjustment benefit.
description:
Oscar Health, the health insurer focused on individual and small group plans, reported net income of $167.3 million for the third quarter of 2026, or $0.49 a diluted share. In the same quarter a year earlier it lost $137.5 million, or $0.53 a share. Revenue was $5.14 billion against $2.99 billion. The company also raised its full-year guidance for the third time this year. This article explains the numbers in Oscar's earnings release, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, what a large risk adjustment benefit means for how to read them, and what it may signal for people who buy health coverage on their own. It is a summary of company-reported results and not investment advice.

The quarter in numbers

Earnings from operations were $178.0 million, against a loss of $129.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, was $206.9 million against a loss of $101.5 million. The medical loss ratio, which is the share of premium revenue spent on medical care, was 84.0% against 88.5%. For the first nine months the ratio was 78.1% against 84.8%. The SG&A expense ratio, which measures administrative and selling costs, was 14.0% against 17.5%, and 14.4% for nine months against 17.3%.

Revenue for the nine months was $14.67 billion against $8.90 billion. Effectuated members, meaning people whose coverage is in force and paid for, were 2,691,885 at September 30, 2026, all in Individual and Small Group, against 2,116,904 a year earlier. Those figures show a business that grew its membership by more than a quarter while its revenue grew by more than two thirds in the quarter, which is consistent with higher premiums per member alongside the added members, although the release does not break that out.

The risk adjustment effect

The most important detail for interpreting the quarter is risk adjustment. This is a program in the Affordable Care Act marketplace that transfers money among insurers depending on the health of the people they cover. An insurer with healthier members pays into the system and one with sicker members receives money. Insurers must estimate these transfers during the year, and the estimates change as more data arrive.

Oscar's release says third-quarter revenue included a $250 million benefit from updated risk adjustment estimates. Without that item, the third quarter would have looked very different, a point that some coverage of the results highlighted. The release reports that risk adjustment transfers were $677.3 million in the quarter against $727.5 million a year earlier, and $2.99 billion for nine months against $1.79 billion. The net risk adjustment payable at September 30 was $2.99 billion against $1.68 billion a year earlier. A payable is money the company expects to owe, which is why the size of the liability and the changes in estimate matter.

The release also reports favorable development of prior-period medical costs of $42 million in the quarter, against $84 million in the third quarter of 2025. Favorable development means claims for earlier periods came in lower than the company had reserved, which adds to income.

Cash, investments and cash flow

Cash and cash equivalents were $4.47 billion at September 30, 2026, up from $2.77 billion at the end of 2025 and $2.15 billion a year earlier. Short-term investments were $3.02 billion and long-term investments were $1.44 billion. Operating cash flow for nine months was $3.51 billion against $0.42 billion a year earlier. Large cash balances in a health insurer partly reflect premiums received before claims are paid and obligations such as the risk adjustment payable, so the figures should not be read as free cash.

Guidance raised again

Oscar updated its 2026 outlook. Revenue is now expected at $19.0 billion to $19.3 billion, up from $18.7 billion to $19.0 billion. The medical loss ratio is expected at 80.5% to 81.5%, against 81.0% to 82.0% before. The SG&A ratio is expected at 15.1% to 15.6%, against 15.6% to 16.1%. Earnings from operations are expected at $850 million to $950 million, against $600 million to $800 million. The chief executive said this was the third increase in the earnings outlook. The release does not give a full-year net income forecast.

Looking toward 2027

The company said its pricing, products and technology position it to grow market share and expand margins in 2027, but gave no numeric targets. The forward-looking statements point to several policy factors that could change results: the federal rules for 2027 benefit and payment parameters, the expiration of enhanced advance premium tax credits, and possible funding for cost-sharing reductions. Those items affect how much people pay for marketplace coverage and how many sign up, which feeds directly into an insurer's membership and the health of its risk pool.

How to read it

A strong quarter with a large one-time-style estimate change is not the same as a steady run rate. The medical loss ratio and expense ratio improvements are real and are consistent across the nine months, which suggests better underlying results than a year earlier. At the same time, a $250 million estimate change is large relative to $167.3 million of net income, so investors and observers will watch whether later quarters confirm the estimates. Risk adjustment is also settled with final data later, so estimates can move again.

What it means for consumers

For people who buy their own coverage, insurer profit does not translate directly into lower premiums. Premiums for next year are set in advance, and the release itself notes that policy changes, including tax credit rules, could alter the market. Shoppers can compare plans during open enrollment on healthcare.gov or their state exchange, and should review networks, deductibles and out-of-pocket limits, not only monthly premiums.

What to watch next

Watch the next release for the size of any further risk adjustment changes, whether the medical loss ratio holds near the new guidance range, and what Oscar says about 2027 pricing and membership. Oscar's filings are on the SEC website. This article summarises public company statements and is not financial or medical advice.

Revenue rose to $5.14 billion from $2.99 billion, and effectuated membership reached 2,691,885 against 2,116,904 a year earlier.

Its swing to profit, and the role of risk adjustment in it, show how sensitive marketplace insurers are to estimates of member health, and how that can ripple into premiums and plan availability for people who buy their own coverage.

title: Mercury General Reports Q3 Loss of $13.7M on Investment Losses
summary: Mercury General reported a third-quarter 2026 net loss of $13.7 million, driven by $261.9 million of pre-tax realized investment losses, while operating income was $193.3 million and the combined ratio was 90.2%, with nine-month net income up 30% to $440.2 million.
description:
Mercury General Corporation reported a net loss of $13.7 million for the third quarter of 2026, or $0.25 a share. In the third quarter of 2025 the company earned $280.4 million, or $5.06 a share. At first glance the quarter looks like a sharp deterioration. The company's own numbers show that the swing came almost entirely from the investment portfolio rather than from insurance operations. This article explains how the quarter breaks down, what the company said, and how to read a loss that sits next to a 90.2% combined ratio. It summarises a company press release filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and is not investment advice.

Where the loss came from

Mercury reported pre-tax realized investment losses of $261.9 million in the third quarter, against gains of $84.5 million a year earlier. After tax, the loss was $206.9 million against a gain of $66.7 million. The press release says the realized losses were primarily caused by large increases in overall market interest rates. When rates rise, the market value of existing bonds falls, and an insurer that sells bonds or recognises losses can book a realized loss even if it intended to hold them.

Because those items are volatile and are not part of the day-to-day business of writing insurance, the company also reports operating income, which excludes net realized investment gains and losses. Operating income was $193.3 million, or $3.49 a diluted share, against $213.7 million, or $3.86, a year earlier, a decline of about 9.6%. So on an operating basis the quarter was lower than last year but strongly positive.

The underwriting picture

Net premiums earned rose 9.6% to $1.55 billion from $1.41 billion. Net premiums written rose 9.2% to $1.64 billion, and direct premiums written rose 8.7% to $1.70 billion. The combined ratio was 90.2% against 87.0% a year earlier. The loss ratio, the share of premium paid out in claims and claim expenses, was 65.8% against 62.6%, and the expense ratio was 24.4%, unchanged. A combined ratio below 100% means that the insurer earned an underwriting profit before counting investment income.

Catastrophe losses, net of reinsurance, were $23 million in the quarter against $29 million a year earlier, a decline of about 21%. So the rise in the loss ratio did not come from a surge in catastrophe losses, according to the press release figures. The release does not explain the cause of the higher loss ratio, so this article does not offer one.

Nine months tell a different story

For the first nine months of 2026, net income was $440.2 million, or $7.95 a share, up 30% from $338.5 million, or $6.11. Operating income was $582.4 million, or $10.52 a share, against $234.9 million, or $4.24, an increase of about 148%. Net premiums earned were $4.50 billion, up 10.7%. The combined ratio for nine months was 89.8% against 99.0% the year before, an improvement of 9.2 points.

The large gap in the nine-month comparison is partly explained by catastrophe losses. Net of reinsurance, they were $191 million in the first nine months of 2026 against $489 million in the first nine months of 2025. The press release says 2026 catastrophe losses were mainly from storms in Oklahoma and Texas, together with adverse reserve development on the Palisades and Eaton wildfires. Favorable prior-year development for nine months was about $102 million, partly offset by adverse homeowners development tied to the wildfires. The figures show the effect that a heavy wildfire year in 2025 had on that year's comparison.

Capital and shareholders

Book value per share was $50.64 at September 30, 2026, up from $43.64 at the end of 2025. The company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.3175 per share, payable on December 31, 2026 to holders of record on December 17, 2026. The release excerpt we reviewed does not report a book value for September 30, 2025, so no year-over-year comparison is given here.

Why net income and operating income can diverge

Insurers hold large bond portfolios to pay future claims. Accounting rules require some changes in value to flow through the income statement, so net income can swing with markets. Operating income is meant to show the performance of the insurance business itself. Neither measure is complete on its own. Net income includes real losses in portfolio value, while operating income can overstate results if it ignores losses that repeat. Readers can check both, and also the combined ratio, which isolates underwriting.

What it means for policyholders

For customers, a quarter like this does not mean a company is in trouble with claims. An insurer's ability to pay claims depends on its reserves, capital and reinsurance, none of which are directly measured by one quarter's net income. Mercury's book value rose over the first nine months, according to the release. Customers who want to check the financial strength of an insurer can look at ratings from agencies such as AM Best, and at their state insurance department's complaint data.

What to watch next

Watch for whether the combined ratio stays near the 90% range, how the company discusses homeowners business in California where wildfire reserves are still developing, and whether bond market moves reverse in the fourth quarter. The company's quarterly filings are available on the SEC website. This article summarises public company statements and is not financial advice.

The swing came from realized investment losses of $261.9 million before tax, which the company attributed mainly to large increases in overall market interest rates.

The quarter shows how an insurer can earn an underwriting profit and still report an accounting loss when bond prices fall, and it is a reminder that headline net income and operating income can tell different stories.

title: Palomar Q3 Premiums Jump 28% to $767M, 2026 Outlook Raised Again
summary: Palomar Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 gross written premiums of $767.0 million, up 28.4%, net income of $65.3 million and a combined ratio of 80.8%, and lifted its 2026 adjusted net income guidance to $280 million to $285 million.
description:
Palomar Holdings, a specialty insurer best known for earthquake coverage, reported third-quarter 2026 gross written premiums of $767.0 million, up 28.4% from $597.2 million a year earlier. Net income rose 27.0% to $65.3 million, or $2.42 a diluted share, and adjusted net income rose 47.4% to $81.3 million, or $3.01 a share. The company raised its full-year guidance again. This article walks through the numbers in its press release, what drove the growth, and the caveats that come with a changing product mix. It summarises company-reported results and is not investment advice.

The headline figures

Gross written premiums are the total premiums the insurer writes before ceding any to reinsurers. At $767.0 million they were up more than a quarter on the year. Net income was $65.3 million against $51.5 million, and diluted earnings per share were $2.42 against $1.87. Adjusted net income, a non-GAAP measure that strips out certain items, was $81.3 million against $55.2 million, and adjusted diluted earnings per share were $3.01 against $2.01.

On returns, annualised return on equity was 26.6% against 23.9%, and adjusted return on equity was 33.1% against 25.6%. Stockholders' equity was $985.0 million against $878.1 million a year earlier. The press release does not report adjusted EBITDA. Palomar repurchased 70,000 shares for $8.9 million in the quarter and declared a quarterly dividend of $0.45 per share, announced October 29 and payable December 2, 2026.

Underwriting ratios

The combined ratio was 80.8% against 78.1%, an increase of 2.7 points, and the adjusted combined ratio was 76.3% against 74.8%. Excluding catastrophe losses, the adjusted combined ratio was 75.1% against 74.0%. The catastrophe loss ratio was 1.2% against 0.8%. All of these are well below 100%, which means underwriting profit before investment income.

Underneath the combined ratio, the two components moved in opposite directions. The loss ratio rose to 41.5% from 32.3%, while the expense ratio fell to 39.3% from 45.8%. A company's ratios can shift with the mix of products. Crop and some other lines carry different loss and expense profiles than earthquake or inland marine, and a very large increase in one line can move the totals. The press release excerpt we reviewed does not offer a full explanation of the loss ratio increase, so readers should not assume a single cause.

Growth by product

Palomar recategorised its products in 2026 and reclassified the prior-year figures, so the comparisons below use the new categories. Crop gross written premiums were $226.7 million against $106.9 million, an increase of 89.3%. Casualty was $176.8 million against $171.0 million, up 3.4%. Inland marine and property were $160.7 million against $141.7 million, up 13.4%. Earthquake was $154.5 million against $149.9 million, up 3.0%. Surety and credit was $48.4 million against $14.7 million, up 228.4%.

These figures show that the company's growth came from newer lines. Earthquake, the product most associated with Palomar, grew by only 3%. Crop provided the largest dollar increase, about $120 million, followed by surety and credit, about $34 million. For readers, this means that comparing the company with its earlier profile requires attention to what it now writes. Crop insurance is seasonal and is affected by weather and commodity prices, so its contribution can vary from quarter to quarter.

Catastrophe events and guidance

The catastrophe loss discussion in the release cited hurricane and flood events in Hawaii and flood events in the Midwest. Total catastrophe losses were small relative to premium, at a 1.2% loss ratio. For the full year, Palomar's guidance is for adjusted net income of $280 million to $285 million, including $8 million to $12 million of catastrophe losses. The chief executive described the quarter as exceptional, pointing to record premiums and adjusted net income, a 16th consecutive earnings beat and the fourth raise to the 2026 adjusted net income guidance this year. He said growth came from all five product categories and credited the specialty portfolio with providing stability across market cycles. Those are management's characterisations.

Why guidance on catastrophe losses matters

Guidance that includes only $8 million to $12 million of catastrophe losses for a year implies a mild catastrophe season. An insurer that writes earthquake and weather-exposed lines can see results move sharply if a large event occurs, since one event can exceed the budget. The guidance should therefore be read as conditional on how the rest of the year unfolds.

How to read the quarter

The strong earnings and high returns are consistent with a company that is growing profitably in niches. Points of caution include the sharp jump in the loss ratio, the reliance on crop premium for much of the growth, and the fact that adjusted figures exclude items that the company chooses to adjust. Readers who want to judge the quality of earnings can compare net income with adjusted net income and read the reconciliation in the press release.

What it means for the market

Specialty insurers tend to do well when standard markets restrict capacity and poorly when price competition returns. Palomar's growth suggests that demand for specialty coverage remains strong. For consumers and businesses, that can mean more options for hard-to-place risks such as earthquake, though prices and terms are set by individual policies and regions.

What to watch next

Watch for the fourth-quarter results and 2027 outlook, how the loss ratio develops as the product mix changes, and whether earthquake growth picks up. The company's filings are on the SEC website. This article summarises public statements and is not financial advice.

Its numbers show where an insurer can grow quickly in a market where many property rates are softening, and how a shift in product mix changes the loss and expense ratios that readers use to judge profitability.

title: Definity Q3: Cat Losses Push Combined Ratio to 100.6%
summary: Definity Financial reported a third-quarter 2026 net loss of $32.4 million after $190.0 million of catastrophe losses lifted its combined ratio to 100.6%, while gross written premiums rose 36.2% to $1.67 billion following the $3.3 billion acquisition of Travelers' Canadian operations.
description:
Definity Financial Corporation, the Canadian property and casualty insurer, reported a net loss of $32.4 million attributable to common shareholders for the third quarter of 2026. A year earlier it earned $193.1 million. The main reason was weather: catastrophe losses of $190.0 million contributed 12.8 points to the combined ratio, which rose to 100.6% from 89.4%. At the same time, premiums grew by more than a third because of its acquisition of the Canadian business of Travelers. This article sets out the figures as reported in the company's results, which were dated November 5, 2026 and summarised by Insurance Business Canada, and explains how to read them. It is not investment advice.

The headline numbers

Operating net income, which management uses to look through some volatile items, was $43.9 million, down from $125.2 million, and operating earnings per share were $0.36. The company recorded an underwriting loss of $8.8 million, compared with underwriting income of $113.6 million a year earlier. Net investment income was $79.3 million against $54.1 million, which helped partly offset the underwriting result.

The combined ratio of 100.6% means that claims and expenses together were slightly more than the premium earned. Catastrophe losses of $190.0 million added 12.8 points to that ratio. Without those catastrophe costs, the ratio would have been about 87.8% on the same figures, though that is our arithmetic and not a number the company reported. The company had earlier flagged a catastrophe hit for July and August, according to Insurance Business Canada.

Property took the hit

The results by line show where the pressure was. Personal property, which covers homes and similar risks, had a combined ratio of 112.1% against 83.6%. Catastrophes added 32.6 points to that line, against 3.6 points a year earlier. Personal auto had a combined ratio of 96.0% against 94.0%. Commercial lines had a combined ratio of 96.1% against 88.1%. In other words, the swing from profit to loss came mostly from homeowners-type exposure to storms, while auto remained profitable on an underwriting basis.

Premium growth from the acquisition

Gross written premiums rose 36.2% to $1.67 billion in the quarter, and to $4.87 billion for the first nine months, up 35.4%. Personal lines grew 36.9% and commercial lines grew 34.2%. Broker channel growth drove most of the gains, while the direct channel grew 4.1%. The growth reflects the completion of the acquisition of Travelers' Canadian property and casualty operations, valued at $3.3 billion. Pro forma, the combined business writes about $6.4 billion in premiums a year, and the company says it is on track for full-year gross written premiums of $6.5 billion.

Chief executive Rowan Saunders said growth came from retaining the acquired renewal book and from underlying growth. This is an important point for an acquisition: the value depends on keeping the customers and brokers that came with the purchased business, and the quarter's premium figures indicate that has largely happened so far.

Synergies and integration

Definity reported run-rate synergies of $56 million, which contributed $14 million to third-quarter earnings. It revised its annual synergy target to $125 million, and chief financial officer Philip Mather said the company expects to capture at least one third of that in 2026. Synergies are cost savings or other benefits from combining two businesses, and they typically take time to realise and carry costs of their own. Readers should view synergy targets as management estimates.

Capital and returns

Trailing twelve-month operating return on equity was 10.3% against 12.5% a year earlier. Book value per share was $34.53, up 3.3% year over year. The company reported financial capacity of about $1.2 billion. Capacity is a measure of money available for growth, acquisitions or buffers, as defined by the company.

How to read a one-quarter loss

Three points help put the quarter in context. First, a net loss attributable to common shareholders can include items that operating income excludes, so the gap between the loss of $32.4 million and operating income of $43.9 million is worth reading in the company's reconciliation. Second, catastrophe losses are lumpy: the same company earned $193.1 million in the third quarter of 2025 when weather was milder. Third, the premium base has changed after the acquisition, so comparing it with last year's figures mixes organic growth with purchased business.

What it means for Canadian homeowners

Insurers respond to rising weather losses through higher rates, changes to deductibles and tighter underwriting. A result like this does not in itself determine what an individual policyholder pays, but it adds to evidence that property insurance is under pressure in parts of Canada. Homeowners can reduce risk and sometimes premiums by checking water and wind coverage, maintaining roofs and sump pumps, and asking their broker how deductibles apply to different kinds of storm damage.

What to watch next

Watch for the fourth-quarter figures, whether personal property combined ratios return to more normal levels, and how much of the $125 million synergy target is captured. Definity publishes results on its investor relations website and on SEDAR+. This article summarises public company statements and is not financial advice.

title: Axis Max Life H1 FY27: VNB Up 21% to Rs 1,180 Crore
summary: Axis Max Life reported first-half FY27 value of new business of Rs 1,180 crore, up 21%, with a VNB margin of 25.4%, up 210 basis points, while its parent Max Financial Services reported profit after tax of Rs 219 crore, up 137%.
description:
Axis Max Life Insurance, one of India's larger private life insurers, reported a 21% rise in value of new business for the first half of the 2026-27 financial year. VNB was Rs 1,180 crore, and the VNB margin was 25.4%, up 210 basis points from a year earlier. The results were announced on October 30, 2026, and the company distributed a press release that was published by the news agency ANI and other outlets. This article explains what those numbers mean, what else the company reported, and what the figures do not tell readers. The release is company-reported and unaudited, and the article is not investment advice.

What VNB and VNB margin measure

Life insurance is a long-term business. A policy sold today will generate premiums and costs over many years, so profit cannot be read from one year's accounts alone. Value of new business is an actuarial estimate of the present value of the profits that policies sold during the period are expected to generate, after allowing for the cost of capital. VNB margin expresses that value as a share of the annualised premium of new business. A higher margin means a larger expected profit per rupee of new sales. In the first half of FY27, Axis Max Life reported a margin of 25.4%, up 210 basis points, which is 2.1 percentage points. The chief financial officer attributed the gain to an improved product mix, according to the release.

Premium growth

The company reported individual adjusted first year premium of Rs 4,368 crore, up 12%. The press release uses this measure and does not report annualised premium equivalent separately. Gross written premium was Rs 18,066 crore, up 17%, and renewal premium was Rs 11,247 crore, up 18%. Renewal premium is money from policies already in force, and strong growth in it reflects the build-up of the in-force book. The chief financial officer said renewal growth drove the 17% increase in gross written premium.

Pure retail protection grew 37% over the first half, according to the release. The release also states that the annuity business grew 130%, but that is a second-quarter figure and not a half-year one. The company launched a product called SMART RISE in the second quarter. The press release does not say how much of the growth came from that product.

Embedded value and returns

Embedded value is another actuarial measure. It estimates the value of a life insurer's existing business plus its net assets. Axis Max Life reported embedded value of Rs 31,437 crore at September 30, 2026, up 17%, and annualised operating return on embedded value of 17.3%, up 100 basis points. Operating return on embedded value shows how much value the business created in a year before economic changes, as a share of the opening value. Embedded value figures depend on assumptions and are calculated by actuaries, which is why they are usually reviewed by an independent consultant.

Market position and the parent

The company said it holds a private-market share of 10.1%. Its listed parent, Max Financial Services, which owns about 80% of the insurer, reported consolidated figures for the half year. Revenue excluding investment income was Rs 17,484 crore, up 16%, revenue including investment income was Rs 26,582 crore, up 17%, and profit after tax was Rs 219 crore, up 137%. That profit figure is the consolidated parent figure, not the standalone profit of the insurer. Axis Bank and its affiliates are shareholders in the insurer, according to the release.

Management commentary

Chief executive Sumit Madan credited the distribution franchise and disciplined execution for the half-year performance. He also described the proposed emphasis by the insurance regulator IRDAI on simpler distribution economics and stronger persistency as a step in the right direction. Persistency measures how many policies are still in force after a given period, and regulators and analysts watch it as a sign of whether customers were sold products that fit them.

What the release does not say

It is worth noting what the source leaves out. It does not report persistency ratios, claim settlement ratio, solvency ratio or assets under management. It does not give the split of premiums by distribution channel, beyond saying that the company is multi-channel. It gives growth rates but not the absolute first-half FY26 figures. Readers who want those details can check the company's disclosures and the regulator's data.

An advertorial source

The primary source for this article is a company press release distributed through a paid distribution service, and the news agency noted it is not responsible for the content. Because of that, we have reported the figures as company statements and have limited ourselves to what the release says. The numbers are unaudited.

What it means for customers

For people buying life insurance, VNB margins are an industry measure and do not tell an individual how good a policy is. What matters for a buyer is the cover, the premium, the claim record and the insurer's solvency. Customers can compare the claim settlement ratio and persistency reported by each insurer in IRDAI's public data, and read the policy document carefully, including exclusions and charges.

What to watch next

Watch for the full-year FY27 results, how the protection business develops, and how any IRDAI changes to distribution rules affect margins. The company publishes its disclosures on its website and on the stock exchanges. This article summarises public company statements and is not financial advice.
